corpus_definition: An area of short green grass in a garden.

forms.definition: an area of short green grass around a house or in a park
forms.example: My father cuts the lawn every Saturday morning.

syn.note: Grass is the plant itself; a lawn is an area of short grass that people look after.
Turf is grass with its earth, often used for sports fields or sold in pieces.
In American English a yard is the land around a house; it may have a lawn in it.

forms.note: There is no verb made from lawn. People say 'mow the lawn' or 'cut the grass'.

context.text: Behind our house in Fergana there is a small lawn with two apple trees. In summer we put a carpet on the lawn and drink tea in the shade.

reviewer_note: Only one family form exists; compounds like lawnmower are left out for the Compounds branch.

corpus_definition: To jump a long way or high into the air.

forms.example: With one leap, the cat was on the roof.
forms.note: Also used for a sudden big change: 'a leap in prices'.

syn.note: Everyday word with the same meaning.
A long jump, often one of many while running.
A small, short jump, often on one foot.

forms.definition: to jump a long way or very high
forms.example: Watch the dog leap over the fence!
forms.note: Past form: leapt (more British) or leaped (more American).

syn.note: Everyday word; leap usually means a bigger, stronger jump.
Jump quickly and suddenly.
Move forward with long jumps.
Make a small, short jump.

context.text: The old cat leapt onto the garden wall. It was a high leap, and all the children clapped.

reviewer_note: Noun is a zero conversion of the verb; compounds leapfrog and leap year left out.

corpus_definition: A long rope used to control a dog while walking.

forms.definition: a long piece of rope or leather for holding a dog
forms.example: Always keep your dog on a leash in the city.
forms.note: Leash is more American; in British English people usually say 'lead'.

syn.note: British English word for the same thing.
Any narrow piece of leather or cloth; a leash is one kind.
A rope is any thick string; a leash is made for dogs.

forms.definition: to tie a dog to a rope or strap so it cannot run away
forms.example: Please leash your dog before you enter the park.

syn.note: Tie is general; leash is only for animals, mostly dogs.

context.text: In Tashkent parks, dog owners must keep their pets on a leash. Madina always leashes her puppy before they cross the busy road.

reviewer_note: American leash vs British lead noted. Unleash (mostly 'unleash anger/power') not shown as a form.

corpus_definition: A formal talk given to a group of students.

forms.definition: a formal talk about a subject to a group of students
forms.example: Our first lecture starts at nine o'clock.

syn.note: Easier and less formal; a talk can be for anyone, not only students.
A speech is a formal talk at an event, not usually to teach.
A talk that shows information, often with slides.
A lesson is a class, often at school, with more activity than listening.

forms.definition: to give formal talks to students, usually at a university
forms.example: She lectures in economics at a university in Samarkand.
forms.note: It can also mean to tell someone angrily how to behave: 'Stop lecturing me!'

syn.note: Teach is general; lecture means teaching by talking to a large group.
General word for talking to people.

people.definition: a person who teaches at a university or college
people.example: My brother is a lecturer at Tashkent State University.

context.text: Dilnoza lectures on history at a university in Bukhara. Every lecture is full, because students love her stories about the Silk Road.

reviewer_note: Verb also has a 'tell someone off' meaning; kept in a note on the conversion entry.

corpus_definition: The power to act or speak without being restricted.

forms.definition: the freedom to live, act and speak as you want
forms.example: Every person has the right to liberty.
forms.note: 'Take the liberty of doing something' = do it without asking first.

syn.note: Everyday word with the same meaning; liberty is more formal.
Freedom from control by another person or country.
Things the law says you are allowed to do or have.

ant.note: Being owned by another person, with no freedom at all.
Being kept in a prison or a cage.

forms.note: Liberate (to set free) comes from the same old Latin root, but it is not made from liberty.
Liberal comes from the same old Latin root, but it is not made from liberty.

context.text: Many people in history fought for liberty. Today we usually say freedom, but you still hear about liberty in law and in important speeches.

reviewer_note: liberate/liberal share the Latin root but are not derived from liberty: listed as not_family.

forms.definition: a cover on the top of a box, pot or jar
forms.example: Put the lid on the pot so the soup stays hot.

syn.note: General word for anything that goes over something.
Easy, everyday word: 'Where's the top of this jar?'
A small lid for a bottle or a pen.

context.text: Grandma lifted the lid of the big pot, and the smell of plov filled the kitchen. Then she put the lid back to keep it warm.

reviewer_note: Only one family form; compound eyelid left out for the Compounds branch.

corpus_definition: The way a person lives their daily life.

forms.definition: the way a person lives, including their work, food and free time
forms.example: Moving to the city changed his whole lifestyle.

syn.note: Phrase with the same meaning; also used for a whole group or country.
Things you do often; your habits are part of your lifestyle.
The things you do every day in the same order.

context.text: My uncle had an unhealthy lifestyle with fast food and no sport. Now he walks every evening, and his new lifestyle makes him feel younger.

reviewer_note: Headword is itself a compound (life + style); no other family forms exist.

corpus_definition: A layer of material used to cover the inside of clothes.

forms.definition: a layer of cloth that covers the inside of a coat, bag or box
forms.example: My winter jacket has a soft, warm lining.
forms.note: Idiom: 'every cloud has a silver lining' = something good can come from a bad situation.

syn.note: Padding is thick and soft; a lining can be thin.
General word for one level of material on or under another.

forms.definition: to cover the inside of something with a layer of material
forms.example: She lined the drawer with clean paper.
forms.note: Line has many other meanings (a line on paper, stand in line); here it means covering the inside.

syn.note: Cover is general; this verb means covering the inside.
Fill or cover with something thick and soft.

forms.definition: having a layer of material on the inside
forms.example: These lined boots keep my feet warm in winter.
forms.note: Lined paper (paper with lines on it) is a different meaning.

syn.note: Padded means with thick soft material inside.

ant.note: With no layer of material inside.

people.definition: a bag or cover that fits inside something to keep it clean
people.example: Put a new plastic liner in the kitchen bin.
people.note: A liner is also a big passenger ship (another meaning).

context.text: Bobur's grandmother lined his old coat with warm wool. Now the lining keeps him warm on cold winter mornings.

reviewer_note: lining comes from the verb line (= cover the inside), not line (= long thin mark); other senses kept to notes.

corpus_definition: Small pieces of waste left on the ground in public places.

forms.definition: pieces of paper, bottles and other rubbish left on the ground
forms.example: Volunteers picked up all the litter in the park.
forms.note: Other meanings: a group of baby animals born at one time; material for a cat's toilet box.

syn.note: British English; rubbish can also be inside your bin, not only on the ground.
American English for rubbish.
American English, often food waste and things in the bin.
General word for things that are not wanted any more.

forms.definition: to drop rubbish on the ground, or to lie untidily all over a place
forms.example: Empty bottles littered the beach after the party.

syn.note: Scatter means throw or spread things over an area.
Fill a place with too many things in an untidy way.

ant.note: Make a place clean and neat.

context.text: After the festival, plastic cups littered the main square. Next morning, students from the college picked up all the litter in big bags.

reviewer_note: Map keeps the 'rubbish' sense; baby-animal and cat-litter senses mentioned only in a note. Compounds litterbug and litter bin left out.

corpus_definition: To find the exact position of something.

forms.definition: the place or position where something or someone is
forms.example: The app shows the exact location of your taxi.
forms.note: 'On location' = filming in a real place, not in a studio.

syn.note: Easy everyday word with the same meaning.
The exact point where something is.
A place where something is built or happens.
Informal: a small particular place.

forms.definition: to find exactly where something or someone is
forms.example: Rescue teams worked all night to locate the missing climbers.

syn.note: Everyday word; locate is more formal and means find the exact place.
Find after searching for a long time.
Find the exact place very accurately.
Find someone or something by following signs or information.

ant.note: Not know where something is any more.

forms.definition: to move to a new place to live or work
forms.example: The company relocated its office to Tashkent.
forms.note: Belongs to locate = put something in a place, not finding where something is.

forms.example: Our hotel is located near the old city of Khiva.
forms.note: Belongs to locate = put or build something in a place, not finding it.

context.text: My phone could not locate the new cafe, so I asked a man in the street. He showed me its exact location on the map.

reviewer_note: located (in a place) and relocate (move) belong to the 'put in a place' sense, shown as other_meaning.
